title: When the Silence Burns
premise: August Almeida has spent thirty years translating other people's words while letting her mother tongue—and her mother's history—slip quietly out of her. At the funeral, a stranger named Beatriz addresses the family by their old name, Almeida da Costa, and reveals that August's mother left behind a house, an unfinished letter, and a sister August never knew existed in the Azores. As August travels to claim and translate the letter, she uncovers why her mother fled, what her silence cost, and how much of the language still lives in her body. The novel ends with August reading the letter aloud at her aunt's kitchen table—in Portuguese, imperfect but whole—choosing inheritance over invisibility.
about_author: Ines Marchetti is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between two languages and one long family silence. She writes about diaspora, memory, and the small betrayals of translation from a coastal town where she keeps her grandmother's dictionary within arm's reach.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: August's POV. Days before the funeral, we see her managing condolences with practiced deflection, translating sympathy into something bearable. A flashback shows her childhood habit of pretending not to understand Portuguese when adults said too much. Emotional beat: grief met with armor; the reader learns invisibility is her oldest skill.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: August's POV. At the funeral, a weathered stranger, Beatriz, calls the family 'Almeida da Costa' and leaves a card with an Azorean address. August's brother dismisses it; August pockets it. That night she catches herself dreaming in Portuguese for the first time in decades. Emotional beat: a crack in the wall—curiosity arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: August's POV, interwoven with fragments of her mother's letters (untranslated). Sorting the estate, August finds a sealed envelope addressed in Portuguese to someone named Filomena, plus a deed to property she never knew of. Her brother wants to sell everything fast. Emotional beat: the tension between closure as erasure and closure as understanding.

chapters.title: What the Ocean Keeps
chapters.summary: August's POV. Against her own instincts, she books a flight to São Miguel. On the plane she attempts to read the letter and discovers how much vocabulary she has lost—words surfacing like drowned things. Arrival: green cliffs, a village where her face is familiar to strangers. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into vertigo and strange homecoming.

chapters.title: Filomena
chapters.summary: August's POV. She meets her aunt Filomena, her mother's older sister, who greets her with the old family name and no surprise—as if she'd been waiting forty years. Filomena feeds her, talks endlessly, and refuses to answer direct questions about why Maria left. Emotional beat: warmth laced with withheld history; belonging offered on someone else's terms.

chapters.title: The Year of the Eruption
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Filomena's memories rendered in close third. The Capelinhos eruption of 1957–58, the family's ruin, the desperate calculus of who emigrates and who stays. We learn Maria was promised to another man before she vanished to the mainland. Emotional beat: the past acquiring weight and texture; survival revealed as a choice made by the young.

chapters.title: Translation Is Betrayal
chapters.summary: August's POV. Filomena finally hands over Maria's full correspondence—decades of letters August's mother sent but never mailed, or that were returned. August begins translating them and falters: every word choice feels like editing her mother's soul. A fight with Filomena over a painful letter. Emotional beat: rising tension—the impossibility of perfect fidelity, in language and in love.

chapters.title: Why She Left
chapters.summary: August's POV, climax building. The final letter reveals the truth: Maria left pregnant by a man her family forbade, choosing shame abroad over a life not her own—and chose silence afterward because telling meant losing everything twice. August recognizes her own smile as inherited architecture. Emotional beat: fury, then devastating compassion; the price of survival made concrete.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: August's POV. Climax. In Filomena's kitchen, with relatives gathered, August reads the last letter aloud in Portuguese—stumbling, searching, sometimes inventing—but aloud, refusing the translator's distance. Halfway through she abandons the page and speaks directly to her mother's memory. Emotional beat: the novel's peak; grief spoken rather than managed, language reclaimed through imperfection.

chapters.title: Almeida da Costa
chapters.summary: August's POV, coda. Months later: she has kept the house, begun teaching herself the lost vocabulary, and signs her first published translation with her full inherited name. Her brother visits, wary, and she gives him a copy of the letters. Final image: August speaking Portuguese on the phone with Filomena, laughing. Emotional beat: resolution—belonging chosen, inheritance accepted, silence ended.
